Synapse also creates write.lock in that directory to coordinate concurrent saves; it contains no project content and does not need to be versioned. Session hooks deliver a compact guide index and an excerpt of the overview, including after compaction. Agents using MCP without a session hook are instructed to request the index at startup; ordinary memory recall also includes the index while the feature is enabled. Complete guide bodies are read on demand through knowledge , in pages of at most 6,000 UTF-8 bytes. The index includes at most 32 guides and an overview excerpt of at most 1,800 bytes. Guides describe the checkout being used. They are not stored as global memories or shared by repository identity across different worktrees. Existing project decisions still belong in memory, and repeatable procedures still belong in skills. Refresh Ask your connected agent: Refresh Synapse's database guide against the current migrations. Preserve my edits and summarize the changes. Synapse compares tracked source hashes whenever the index or a guide is requested. A guide marked needsreview has changed, missing, or unreadable source files. A guide marked unchecked reached the per-request source budget; its unchecked count tells you how many sources remain unverified. Treat both states as requiring source inspection. current means those tracked files match; it does not prove the explanation is accurate or account for newly added files that were never tracked. Source code remains authoritative. Refresh is explicit. Synapse does not rewrite guides when a source changes. The agent must read the existing guide and supply its revision when saving. If another agent or a person edited it in the meantime, Synapse refuses the save until the agent rereads and reconciles the changes. The revision protects against an intervening edit; review the agent's diff to confirm it preserved the intent of your text. Names contain lowercase letters and digits. Guides require 1–64 inspected repository-relative source files, with a 2 MiB limit per source and a 16 MiB aggregate source-read budget per request. Guide bodies are limited to 128 KiB. Credential files and Synapse metadata cannot be tracked sources, and recognized credentials in generated text are rejected. These checks do not replace reviewing what an agent writes. Resource use and filesystem access Knowledge work runs only when requested or handed over at session startup. There is no watcher, polling loop, background model, or persistent source cache. Disabling the setting skips guide access entirely. Each request streams source hashes through a 64 KiB buffer and hashes shared files once, even when multiple guides reference them. The index examines at most 128 directory entries and 32 guide files, caps source reads at 16 MiB, and limits serialized index output to 32 KiB. Oversized or unverified input is reported instead of silently being treated as current. At most two knowledge jobs run at once per process; additional requests receive a retry message. Filesystem work runs outside the async executor. A busy writer also returns a retry message rather than waiting indefinitely. Knowledge access is restricted to the project root supplied to the MCP process through SYNAPSE_PROJECT_DIR , falling back to its starting directory. A tool may pass that root or a folder inside it, but it cannot use Synapse to read or write guides in another checkout. Guide paths and source components cannot be symlinks. On Unix, access and atomic writes use pinned directory handles, so replacing a directory with a symlink during a request cannot redirect that operation outside the opened repository. On Windows, directory handles are held without delete sharing and reparse-point files are rejected. Source files must be regular files; pipes and other special files are rejected. Metadata errors do not echo document contents, and overview excerpts are redacted before truncation. To repeat the synthetic performance check in a disposable repository: sh Copy CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_BUILD_OVERRIDE_STRIP=none CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_STRIP=none \ cargo run --manifest-path crates/synapsecore/Cargo.toml --release --example knowledge It measures an empty index and 32 guides referencing the same 64 source files (4 MiB total), reporting median and 95th-percentile latency, bytes read, and response size. These are local synthetic measurements, not a guarantee for slow or remote filesystems. Disable Choose Settings → Project Knowledge → Off , or run: sh Copy synapse settings knowledge off Synapse immediately refuses further knowledge-tool calls and stops including guides in new session handoffs and memory recall. Restart connected tools to remove the tool definitions and guidance from their next session. Context already delivered to an active agent cannot be withdrawn. Existing Markdown files remain in the repository and are still available through ordinary file access.

title: The memory map
description: How the memory map lays out projects, supersession, and shared vocabulary.
text: The map is the store drawn as a graph: one node per memory, one per project, and links between them. It answers what a list cannot — which projects this machine holds anything about, where the weight is, and what a decision sits next to. It is built by synapsecore::brain::map , which reads and lays out; both dashboards draw the result. No model, no network service, no second index, and no state of its own. The display reads at most the newest 160 memories and reports that limit when the store is larger. It is an inspection view, not a complete relevance ranking. What is on it Nodes. One per memory, plus one hub per project and one for global memory. A memory's node carries its opening line as a label, the hub it belongs to, and how many links touch it. Superseded memories are on the map, drawn hollow: they are out of recall, still in the store, and still restorable. Links. Three kinds, and only one of them is inferred. Link Meaning Source Scope This memory belongs to that project, or to global memory. Recorded Supersedes This memory was replaced by that one. Recorded Shared Both memories use enough of the same uncommon words. Inferred A supersession is drawn only when both memories are on the map; a line to a node that is not there is worse than no line. Shared links use the stoplist recall uses, so a search and a map cannot disagree about which words mean nothing. Two memories are linked when they share at least two words of four characters or more, counting the first forty words of each; every memory keeps its three strongest, and a pair is drawn once however many times it is chosen. Three dimensions The layout is a volume, not a plane. On a plane a cluster with more neighbours than the plane has room for either overlaps itself or shoves everything else off the map, and both of those are the layout lying about the store; in a volume it uses the third direction instead. The coordinates are the unit cube, y downward and z toward the viewer. The window turns it. Drag to turn, scroll to move closer or further out — toward whatever the pointer is over, not the middle — and shift-drag to slide the cloud in the frame. Nearer nodes are drawn larger and brighter, which is the only depth cue a still frame has. Reset view puts the camera back where it started. The terminal draws the front of the same cloud, which is where the window's camera starts: the same picture, before anybody turned it. Depth there decides only what is drawn over what, since a cell holds one character. Past sixty memories it leaves the inferred links out and says so in its title — the window draws them at a tenth of the opacity of a recorded link, and a braille cell has no tenth to spend. What it costs Everything is bounded, because a page that costs a second to open is a page nobody opens twice. 160 memories are read and laid out, newest first. Both surfaces read that constant rather than choosing one, so neither shows a different half of the same store. The page reports both numbers whenever the store is larger. Inferred links are capped per memory, so a store where everything resembles everything draws hundreds of lines rather than the twelve thousand a full pairing would. The layout is a fixed number of passes over a fixed number of nodes, seeded deterministically. The same store opens onto the same map every time: a map is worth having because its shape is learnable, and one that settled differently on a slower machine would be two maps. Turning the map re-projects and repaints; it never lays out again. The layout is the expensive half and it does not depend on where you are looking from. Nothing is stored. The map is read when the page is opened and again when it is refreshed, never held and redrawn from a store that has moved on. Reading it in either surface The desktop paints the whole map into one canvas — quads for the nodes, stroked paths for the links, through the same pipeline guise::GpuView submits to. It is painted rather than laid out because a node's size, its opacity, and the order it is drawn in all depend on where the camera is, and that is arithmetic rather than layout. A click is answered by projecting the same points again and taking the nearest circle the pointer landed in; it reads that memory by id and opens it beside the map — by id, because the map covers the whole store while the memory list covers one search. The plot is dark whatever the theme is. A glow is light added to what is behind it, and on a light background there is nothing to add to: every halo reads as a smudge. The page around it stays the user's theme. The terminal draws the same coordinates in braille. A terminal cannot hover, so the cursor keys walk the nodes and whatever the cursor lands on is spelled out underneath. SYNAPSE_PAGE=map opens the desktop app straight onto it. Fixtures Run from crates/synapsecore : sh Copy cargo test brain::graph cargo test --lib tui The graph fixtures check hub assignment and naming, that a supersession off the map draws nothing, that shared words link related memories and common words link nothing, the per-memory cap, label extraction, that a bounded map reports what it left out, that every node lands inside the unit cube, that two runs place every node identically, that the cloud has real depth rather than being a plane with a third number attached, and that nodes are spread rather than stacked. The terminal fixtures draw every page at sizes down to one cell by one, because a panic inside a draw happens with the terminal already in raw mode.

title: Retrieval checks
description: Ranking, drift, exact UTF-8 paging, relevance checks, and reproducible performance fixtures.
text: Recall finds relevant memories within the configured budget. readmemory reads the exact stored body of one hit in bounded pages. Both apply the same global plus current-project scope and exclude superseded records. Neither requires a model or network service. Recall searches two FTS5 indexes over the same rows: memory , stemmed with porter unicode61 over body and source (source weighted 0.3), and memorygram , a contentless trigram index kept in step at every write. Each ranks the query on its own and the two lists are merged by reciprocal rank fusion ( K = 60 ). When a hit has to be abridged, recall sends its opening line if that holds a matched word and the FTS5 snippet around the match otherwise. readmemory reads by id and uses neither index. Every query term is an OR, so a memory sharing one word with a long question still matches. Recall counts how many of the query's terms each candidate holds and drops any holding fewer than half as many as the best one, before applying the limit. The best match always survives, so a question with a weak answer still gets it. memory list and --explain show every match. Drift Recall and the session hook check what they hand over: a path the memory names that is gone from the checkout (stale), two memories that say opposite things or carry different numbers (conflict), two memories that say the same thing (duplicate). Recall returns everything and lists findings in drift . When a newer memory contradicts a returned one but didn't match the query, recall quotes it. The session hook leaves stale memories and the older half of a conflicting or duplicate pair out of what it injects, and says so. remember reports what a new memory contradicts or repeats. synapse memory drift runs the check on everything a folder can see. Nothing is superseded or deleted automatically. Relative paths are only checked for project memory in its own checkout. Paths under another account's home, temp folders, and build output are never called missing. Exact reading Call readmemory with the id and project from a recall. Start at offset zero, then pass each returned next as the next offset until it is null. Offsets and total are UTF-8 byte counts. Concatenating the page bodies reconstructs stored text without compaction, ellipses, or broken characters. Lean limits a body page to 2,800 bytes. Balanced and Full limit it to 6,000 bytes. These byte bounds also fit within the configured character budget. Source labels have a separate 240-byte allowance with sourceabridged marking truncation; metadata and JSON framing are additional to the body allowance. SQLite selects only the requested body slice, so paging does not allocate the whole memory in the server. Missing, superseded, and out-of-scope ids all return a null memory. An offset beyond a visible body's end or inside a UTF-8 character is an error. The exact end returns an empty body and null next . Pages read current data; restart at zero if the memory is edited between requests. Owner-facing CLI inspection and restore remain available for hidden history. The MCP tool is also available through bridges that discover the server's tool list. Existing user guidance is preserved; the server supplies the reading hint at initialization when it is absent. Correctness fixtures Run from crates/synapsecore : sh Copy cargo test --test retrieval --test mcp The retrieval fixtures check opposing statements, changed numbers and short identifiers, exact duplicates, Unicode search, scope isolation, supersession and restore, every budget combination, and lossless paging of long text containing code, whitespace, multibyte characters, and embedded NULs. Protocol tests exercise the complete recall-to-read flow through the released tool schema. Approximate wording overlap cannot establish that two facts are equivalent. Balanced and Lean retain exact-body deduplication but no longer suppress distinct bodies by word-set similarity. Only explicit supersession establishes a correction; drift findings point at candidates for one. tests/bias.rs scores the relevance floor against an unfloored search on a labeled corpus (no answer lost or moved down; surplus beside each answer falls from 5.1 to 0.9 memories) and checks that an unmarked correction is always flagged when its outdated memory comes back. Performance fixture sh Copy cargo run --release --example retrieval -- 10000 30 cargo run --release --example retrieval -- 100000 30 The arguments are memory count and measured iterations, defaulting to 10,000 and 30. They are bounded at one million memories and one thousand iterations. The fixture creates and removes its own temporary database; it never opens the user's store, changes settings, or connects to a network service. Output is JSON containing build profile, seed time, database-open time, database bytes, and p50/p95/max latency plus structured response bytes for: selective recall: a term in every thousandth memory; common-term recall: a term present throughout the store; recent scoped recall: the newest visible memories; exact reading: the first bounded page of one memory. The corpus is deterministic and all-global, with approximately 240-byte bodies. Each operation has one untimed warmup. Timings include library calls and JSON serialization, but exclude process startup, transport framing, model/client processing, and fixture generation. The database-open measurement includes verification after seeding, with OS file caches still warm. Response sizes count structured JSON once; MCP transports may carry a text representation as well. Use release builds and record the machine alongside results. Compare the same fixture before and after a change. The fixture exposes scaling trends; it does not simulate cold disks, mixed-project query plans, long-duration memory growth, or semantic relevance on real user questions. Timing thresholds are deliberately absent from shared-runner correctness tests. Relevance Before changing ranking or adding inference, measure recall quality on representative questions: sh Copy synapse memory eval cases.toml --budget lean Each [[case]] names a query , an optional project folder, and expect : text a useful memory contains, or nothing for a question no memory answers. The report gives the share ranked first, the share found, MRR, the share whose answer text survived the response budget, and noise on unanswerable cases. Run it on a copy of a real store ( SYNAPSE_DATA pointed at the copy, never the live folder) before and after the change, and keep resource cost in view alongside it.

title: Security, stability, and resource review
description: Technical documentation for Security, stability, and resource review.
text: Reviewed on 2026-10-26. Scope: Project Knowledge, its MCP/session integration, and the three dependency lockfiles. This is a source review and local validation, not a penetration test or a benchmark of the entire desktop app. Fixes Redact the complete overview before taking an excerpt. Truncating first could expose the beginning of a credential or cut a private marker in half. Return generic metadata errors instead of parser diagnostics containing document text. Bound invalid-file warnings and serialized index size. On Unix, open guides, sources, and locks through pinned directory handles with no-follow and regular-file checks. Atomic replacement and directory enumeration use those same handles. A directory replaced by a symlink cannot redirect the operation. Pipes cannot block file reads. On Windows, retain ancestor directory handles without delete sharing, reject reparse points, and check the opened file's metadata. Restrict knowledge reads and writes to the MCP process's project root. A connected client cannot use Synapse's filesystem authority to reach another checkout. Use a nonblocking exclusive writer lock. Contention returns a retry response rather than tying up a session indefinitely. Existing revision checks remain in place. Stream source hashes through a 64 KiB buffer, deduplicate hashes within each request, and cap total source reads at 16 MiB. There is no cache across calls, so same-size edits are rechecked. Guides with unverified sources report unchecked instead of current . Limit index inspection to 128 directory entries and 32 guides; cap serialized catalog output at 32 KiB. Keep full guide reads paginated. Execute knowledge filesystem work on the blocking pool, with at most two jobs per process and no unbounded waiting queue. No watcher or periodic scan was added. Disabled knowledge does not inspect guide files. Bound scene packs to 128 within a 256-entry scan, stream manifest reads under 64 KiB, and recheck an opened image asset before decoding it. Presence slot selection uses sets, avatar polling fetches only visible identities, and avatar preferences expire after one year with a 4,096-row hard cap. Dependency updates Updated compatible patch versions where present in each lockfile: Package Patched version h2 0.4.16 quinn-proto 0.11.18 rustls 0.23.46 rustls-webpki 0.103.16 webpki-roots 1.0.10 tokio 1.53.3 chacha20 0.10.2, replacing a yanked version The configured RustSec audit reports zero vulnerabilities in all three lockfiles. The core and sync server have no advisory warnings after these updates. The desktop lockfile still has 13 upstream maintenance-warning entries. Two existing suppressions remain for quick-xml 0.30: RUSTSEC-2026-0194 and RUSTSEC-2026-0195. An audit without those suppressions confirms both advisories. They are retained for GPUI's optional xcb build dependency; cargo tree --target all -i quick-xml@0.30.0 --locked --offline reports no dependency in the currently enabled graph. No additional suppression was introduced. Updating that optional graph requires an upstream-compatible dependency change. Synthetic resource measurements Optimized local benchmark, 40 index requests, disposable fixture with 32 guides sharing 64 source files (4 MiB total): Measurement Result Empty index median / p95 0.32 / 0.48 ms Populated index median / p95 15.58 / 17.11 ms Source bytes read per populated request 4 MiB, down from 128 MiB without deduplication Serialized populated index 7,771 bytes Benchmark process maximum RSS 7,241,728 bytes, about 6.9 MiB RSS includes fixture generation and the benchmark process; it is not the desktop app's memory usage. The benchmark used optimized code with release stripping disabled to avoid a local macOS SQLx procedural-macro loader error. These numbers are filesystem- and machine-dependent; network or unhealthy filesystems can take longer. The read budget bounds bytes and concurrency, not kernel I/O latency. Process-local limits also do not impose a machine-wide cap across independently launched agents. Validation Full headless core, desktop/workspace, and sync-server test suites. MCP end-to-end create/read/disable behavior and session handoffs. Regression tests for redaction boundaries, private content, parser errors, invalid-file floods, per-request byte limits, source deduplication, lock contention, replaced directories, special files, and symlinked locks. A current-thread Tokio test verifies that occupied knowledge workers do not block the async executor and that a third job is refused while two are active. Strict Clippy and formatting checks for the affected workspaces. Windows core cross-compilation with a local Zig C compiler. Windows native runtime and filesystem behavior were not exercised on a Windows machine in this review.

title: Scenes and plugins
description: Technical documentation for Scenes and plugins.
text: Open Scenes in the desktop sidebar. Every MCP session connected to this build gets its own room, including sessions that have not joined the mesh. Restart existing harnesses after updating Synapse so their MCP processes can publish presence. Connections indicate configured harnesses; scene rooms indicate running MCP transports. Two sessions using the same harness get separate rooms. The server sends a heartbeat every ten seconds; an ungraceful exit becomes disconnected after 45 seconds. Graceful exits dim the room immediately. Rooms remain visible for up to a day and are reused on reconnect by harness, project folder, and room slot. Character choices survive reconnects. Click a room to inspect its harness, project, last heartbeat, reported state, and task note. Previous and Next select its character. Filter by project or pause animation. A live connection with no work report displays Connected , not Working. Working, waiting, blocked, and finished poses follow mesh reportstatus calls. The mesh can remain off when only connection presence is needed. On macOS, Reduce Motion pauses animation by default unless you saved a different preference. Pause stops animation; presence continues updating every two seconds. Leaving Scenes stops its reads and animation. Add a scene plugin Choose Open plugins folder . Create a lowercase directory for your pack and put a plugin.toml inside it. Choose Reload plugins to discover it. No rebuild or restart is required. The default location is the Synapse application data directory's plugins folder. SYNAPSE_DATA relocates it along with the rest of Synapse's data. toml Copy api = 1 id = "moonforge" name = "Moon forge" version = "1.0.0" kind = "scene" [scene] floor = "#87959c" wall = "#464d68" wood = "#61576c" accent = "#b5d8df" # Optional room art, exactly 144 by 104 pixels: # background = "room.png" # Optional character sheet, eight characters in a 4 by 2 grid: # characters = "characters.png" framewidth = 26 frameheight = 36 A character occupies three frame columns and four direction rows: down, left, right, up. The sheet therefore has twelve columns and eight rows of frames. Without a custom sheet, the renderer uses the bundled character set. A single custom sheet provides eight appearances repeated across the 32 character slots. Optional background artwork replaces the room's walls, floor, furniture, and props. The renderer overlays occupants and state effects; leave the central bench, fireplace at the upper right, and lower-left delivery area clear for these. API 1 scene plugins are declarative packs: palettes, room art, and character sheets. Synapse owns room layout, session identity, state, animation timing, and selection. Packs cannot execute scripts or read memories, credentials, or files outside their own directory. This is the first plugin capability; it is not a general-purpose code extension runtime. Plugin IDs must contain only lowercase letters and digits, be unique, and cannot replace the included workshop . Unknown fields, unsupported APIs or kinds, invalid colors, missing assets, path traversal, and symlinks outside a pack are rejected. Images must be PNG files up to 16 MiB and 4096 pixels per dimension; manifests are limited to 64 KiB. One invalid plugin does not prevent other scenes from loading. Image decoding errors appear when selecting the scene. The selected scene and animation preference are saved locally. Artwork in source builds The default room is original procedural pixel art. The optional Time Fantasy character sheets are read at build time from assets/scene/characters/chara2.png through chara5.png , copied from the owner's Tink purchase. The build embeds the available sheets, so the executable does not depend on the original asset directory. Keep paid source artwork out of public source distributions. Attribution is finalbossblues, Time Fantasy RPG Sprites 1: https://finalbossblues.itch.io/tf-rpg-charactersprites-1. A checkout without the optional pack builds with a small original character sprite. No artwork is downloaded during build or rendering. Custom scene packs can provide their own appropriately licensed art.

title: What launching costs
description: A measured startup snapshot and the fixtures needed to make a fresh comparison.
text: Measurement snapshot, not a release benchmark or latency guarantee. The figures below describe the measured setup at the time of that investigation. Re-run the fixtures on the release and machine being compared before quoting new results. Numbers from an Apple silicon Mac, release build, a store of 220 memories, with Claude Code, Codex and Ainz installed and connected. They are here so that a change can be compared against something rather than described. The window Time from exec to the first painted frame: about 200ms , of which Synapse's own reads are about 6ms . Phase Cost Whose Process start, dyld, gpui framework init ~85ms the platform Dashboard::new — one Brain::glance , every setting, one memory list ~6ms ours Window creation, Metal pipeline setup ~75ms the platform First frame ~35ms the platform After the frame: tool detection, import scan, integrity check ~60ms ours, deferred The split is the design. Dashboard::new reads only what the first frame needs. Everything whose cost belongs to another program runs in Dashboard::opened , scheduled by window.on_next_frame : Tool detection. Every installed coding agent is asked for its --version , and several start a Node or Bun process to answer. This is unbounded from Synapse's side — it is somebody else's startup time — and it used to be the first thing that happened. The import scan , which walks Claude's and Codex's own memory folders and previews them against this store. Only the Memory page shows the result. The skill survey , which walks the library and every tool's skill folder. One Brain::open , whose whole-file integrity check is worth paying once a session and not before there is a window. Detection also runs one thread per descriptor. The work is waiting, not computing, so waiting in sequence adds the answers up; synapse status and the the terminal fallback is now text-only. A page that has not looked yet has to say so. An empty tool list reads as no tools found , which is a different and much worse statement than not looked yet — hence probed , the "Looking for your tools…" line, and the dash in place of a count. One runtime, one worker, made on first use ( ui/runtime.rs ). A Runtime::new() per call site builds a multi-threaded runtime — a worker per core, spawned and joined again — and the window did that eight times before it existed, for a handful of SQLite queries. The hooks statusline runs on every turn of every session and session on every start, so both are measured with a real payload on stdin — the shape a tool actually sends: Command Cost synapse version (the process floor) 9ms synapse statusline 11ms synapse session 13ms synapse status 13ms Two to four milliseconds of work over the cost of starting a process at all. They read through glance , so no launch reads the whole database to check it. Measure with stdin closed and you will see two seconds: that is INPUTWAIT , the deliberate wait for a client that opened the pipe and has not written yet. It is not the hook being slow, and a benchmark that forgets it is measuring its own test harness. Doing this again sh Copy cargo build --release # window, from a scratch store SYNAPSE_DATA=/tmp/scratch/data SYNAPSE_HOME=$HOME ./target/release/synapse # hooks, with the payload a tool sends echo '{"cwd":"'$PWD'"}' | ./target/release/synapse-cli statusline Never point a dev build at the real data directory: it migrates the store to whatever schema that build carries, and every older Synapse on the machine then refuses to open it.

title: The core library
description: The shipped core library, its public modules, storage boundary, and independent build.
text: synapsecore is the implementation behind Synapse's desktop app, CLI, terminal dashboard, and MCP server. The extraction is complete: all non-drawing behavior lives in crates/synapsecore , and crates/synapse adds the native window. Workspace boundaries The repository has three independent Cargo workspaces: Workspace Responsibility Validation Repository root Native desktop and shared sync types cargo build --locked crates/synapsecore Memory, vaults, mesh, skills, setup, imports, CLI, MCP cargo test --locked crates/synapseserve Optional opaque sync log server cargo test --locked A root test does not exercise the other workspaces. Core resolves independently of the desktop dependency graph and has no dependency on the window or its UI library. The desktop and core package versions stay equal because they ship as one product; synapse version reads the core package version. Public modules The library's public surface is declared in crates/synapsecore/src/lib.rs . Modules Responsibility brain , database Scoped memory, retrieval, exact reading, migrations, integrity, backups imports , learning , usage Reviewed imports, feedback and drift resolutions, usage accounting vault , shellsetup Credential metadata, sealed values, approved scopes, shell environments agent , files , instructions Tool descriptors, managed configuration writes, shared guidance skill , sources , servers Skill and MCP server libraries and their sources relay Mesh messages, roles, teams, process supervision mcp , cli Protocol and command adapters sync Client operations for the optional encrypted replication protocol These are the actual modules, rather than the smaller module set proposed by the original extraction plan. Core includes command and process orchestration as well as storage. Embedding the crate does not make it a sandbox. Storage and concurrency brain::Brain::open opens a local database through the same migration and integrity boundary used by the product. Brain::glance is the lighter opening path used for initial display. Keep handles alive while using the store; they retain the database's advisory lock. Several local MCP processes can share the same brain.db . SQLite WAL coordinates reads, and competing memory writes are queued through the database write path. A backup or restore still needs the lifecycle guards. Use the library or the CLI instead of directly editing tables: indexes, scope metadata, supersession, redaction, imports, and sync identities must stay consistent. Memory is plaintext locally. Credential values use a separate encrypted store or macOS Keychain. Database snapshots do not include those values. Minimal build From the repository root: sh Copy cargo build --release --locked --manifest-path crates/synapsecore/Cargo.toml ./crates/synapsecore/target/release/synapse-cli help For a Rust consumer, use the path to the library workspace: toml Copy [dependencies] synapsecore = { path = "../synapse/crates/synapsecore", default-features = false } The crate currently declares no optional Cargo features. The no-default-features gate verifies that this independent build stays valid; it is not a promise that command, protocol, or platform dependencies are removed. Verification sh Copy cd crates/synapsecore cargo test --locked cargo check --locked --no-default-features cargo test --locked --test cli --test mcp See Embedding for the transport choice and a scoped Rust example, Retrieval checks for ranking and exact-read fixtures, and Developing Synapse for the complete repository gates.

title: Encrypted sync
description: The optional encrypted replication library and opaque log server, with current setup limitations.
text: Synapse includes an optional encrypted replication client in synapsecore::sync , wire types in synapsesync , and an opaque log server in synapseserve . Ordinary memory, recall, skills, and credential scopes work without any of them configured. Current availability The replication code is a library capability. The app and public CLI currently provide no sync setup, pairing, or background-sync flow. Running a log server alone does not connect your desktop to it. Do not edit the live SQLite settings to simulate a setup flow. Rust integrations can use the sync module's Config , push , pull , and once functions. once returns no summary when the store has no complete configuration. An integration is responsible for configuring and protecting its client state. What crosses the network Clients seal memory operations before they leave the machine. The server stores opaque envelopes in an append-only sequence; it cannot search memory, inspect its contents, or resolve conflicts. Clients apply received operations locally. The wire contract calls for a stable repository key rather than an absolute checkout path. An integration must verify its project identities before syncing; the library push operates on the configured store. Use a store whose project memories have portable repository identities. Path-keyed folders are not portable project data. Secret values, local scope approvals, installed tool configuration, worker state, and learning evidence are outside this memory replication contract. The content key protects memory from the server. It does not encrypt the local memory store, which remains plaintext to the local account. Server configuration Build the server from its own workspace: sh Copy cargo build --release --locked --manifest-path crates/synapseserve/Cargo.toml Provide configuration through the service manager's environment. Never put the token in a command argument, repository, or log. Variable Meaning Default SYNAPSESERVE_TOKEN Required shared access token None; startup refuses an empty token SYNAPSESERVE_DATA SQLite log file synapseserve.db SYNAPSESERVE_ADDR Listen address 127.0.0.1:8787 Run crates/synapseserve/target/release/synapseserve under that configured service. GET /health returns ok . POST /push and POST /pull authenticate access to a tenant's log. The protocol number is independent of package versions; requests must match it. Repeated operations are idempotent within their log. The binary serves plain HTTP on loopback. Terminate TLS before exposing it to a network: encrypted envelopes protect memory bodies, but the bearer access token still needs transport protection. The server has request and batch limits; plan retention and disk capacity for its append-only log. Recovery and limitations A server outage leaves local memory available. Keep independent local backups; the log is replication infrastructure, not a complete backup of the installation. A database export excludes credential values and other files needed to rebuild an installation. Supersession relationships currently remain local. A memory superseded on one machine may still be live on another; the wire format does not carry the replacement relation. Review corrections on every participating device. Sync and federation Sync moves one person's memory between their own devices. Federation would query another party's explicitly published knowledge. It is a separate proposal, not a shipped command or a feature of the blind log server. See the Federation proposal for that design's status and trust model. Verification sh Copy cargo test --locked --manifest-path crates/synapseserve/Cargo.toml cargo test --locked --manifest-path crates/synapsecore/Cargo.toml --test sync The protocol and encryption fixtures live in crates/synapsesync ; root Cargo tests cover that workspace member.

title: Windows
description: Build the Windows x64 installer and verify its desktop, CLI, and storage behavior.
text: Synapse builds for Windows x64 with the MSVC Rust toolchain. The desktop needs Direct3D 11. The CLI is packaged separately and works without a graphics session. Build an installer Install Rust stable for x86_64-pc-windows-msvc , Visual Studio Build Tools with Desktop development with C++ and a Windows SDK, and Inno Setup 6. The SDK must include fxc.exe ; set GPUI_FXC_PATH if GPUI cannot find it. From PowerShell at the repository root: powershell Copy powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\packaging\windows\build.ps1 The script builds both binaries with a static C runtime and writes dist\<version>\synapse.<version>.windows.x64.exe and sha256sums.txt . Use -NoBuild to package binaries already built with the same target and flags. CARGO_TARGET_DIR is supported. The release workflow builds and uploads this installer before publishing a release. Windows installers currently ship unsigned. The installer runs per user without elevation, creates a Start menu shortcut, and offers a desktop shortcut and user PATH entry. It installs the app under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Synapse , with the CLI in bin\synapse.exe . Open a new terminal after installation to use synapse by name. Uninstall removes the program and the PATH entry it added, preserving user data. The installer includes the pi extension. Windows connections use that bundled package; SYNAPSE_PI_PACKAGE still overrides its source for development. Synapse stores its database, encrypted vault, and shared guidance under %LOCALAPPDATA%\synapse . The encrypted vault is the Windows backend; Apple's Keychain backend is available only on macOS. Windows editor defaults to Notepad. Bash, zsh, and fish activation hooks are for those shells; Windows users can use synapse run -- <program> <arguments> for credential injection. Verify powershell Copy cargo test --locked cargo test --locked --manifest-path crates/synapsecore/Cargo.toml powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\packaging\windows\smoke.ps1 -Cli "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\Synapse\bin\synapse.exe" The smoke check uses synthetic data in an isolated temporary directory. It verifies memory, vault injection, backup and restore, and repeatable CLI installation. The CI workflow runs the desktop and core suites on Windows.

title: Tutorials
description: Eleven guided walkthroughs arranged by how far into Synapse you are, from a first connection to running agent teams and removing everything cleanly.
text: These are arranged by how far into Synapse you are, not by feature. Each level assumes the one before it, and each tutorial ends by pointing at the next. If you are new, start at the top and stop whenever Synapse is doing what you need — most people never leave the second level, and that is a complete way to use it. Level 1 · Newcomer You have downloaded Synapse and want one tool remembering things. Roughly an hour for both. Install and connect your first tools Start from the release archive, install the CLI, connect Codex, Claude Code, or pi, and verify all three MCP tools from the app, the terminal, and the tool itself. Carry one decision between tools Store a confirmed convention in one tool, end the session, recover it in another, and inspect the exact record that made it across. Level 2 · Daily driver Synapse is connected and you use it every day. This level is about controlling what it remembers, what it can hand to a command, and what your tools know how to do. Curate and optimize memory Add, find, correct, delete, and budget durable memory using both human-readable and JSON output. The one to read if recall is returning too much or the wrong thing. Use a scoped secret in either shell mode Create a vaulted value, compare one-command and ambient loading without printing the value, and watch trust invalidate when the file changes. Keep one skill library across every tool Write an Agent Skill once, install it into every connected tool, and see how Synapse tells a library that moved on from a copy somebody edited by hand. Let your agents write skills Let a session write down a procedure it worked out, prove for yourself that it reaches no tool until you approve it, then correct it and take the correction back. Level 3 · Team operator You want several agents working at once on one job. This is the deepest level, and the one where agents touch real files on your machine — use a checkout you can restore. Start a tool with everything in place Open a tool with memory, scoped credentials, and the project root already wired, without writing anything into that tool's own configuration. Run a team of agents and drive it yourself Turn on the mesh, open a team, read what every agent is doing from one terminal, answer a worker that gets stuck, and shut it all down cleanly. Hand a job to one agent and watch it grow a team Describe an outcome instead of picking a roster, answer the question only you can answer, and reach a worker directly without going through the agent that started it. Level 4 · Maintainer You are responsible for the store staying sound, or you are handing the machine on. Read these before you need them. Export and restore safely Create a validated snapshot, make a reversible change, acquire the exclusive lifecycle lock, restore, and verify recovery. Check, migrate, and remove Synapse Read a full health report, understand what a schema migration does, disconnect one tool, and remove everything while keeping your memory and your own files. What every tutorial includes Each one names its prerequisites, builds one complete outcome, includes verification you can observe rather than assume, calls out the security boundary it crosses, and ends with cleanup or the next safe step. Commands assume the installed synapse CLI is on PATH . If you need exact command syntax outside a guided workflow, use the CLI reference . If a step fails, stop there and use Troubleshooting rather than skipping a trust or integrity check — those checks are the reason the destructive steps later are safe.

title: Install and connect your first tools
description: Go from the signed release archive to a working local MCP connection, and verify the same memory from the desktop app, the terminal, and the coding tool itself.
text: Outcome and prerequisites You will install Synapse, install its command-line tool, connect at least one coding tool, store one harmless memory, and see that same record through three separate surfaces. By the end you will also know exactly which files were touched and how to take every one of them back. For this desktop walkthrough: an Apple-silicon Mac running macOS 13 or later. Linux users can follow the terminal setup guide , then try a memory handoff . Codex, Claude Code, or both installed and on PATH . The latest synapse.zip release archive. About twenty minutes. Move the app somewhere permanent, then open it Extract synapse.zip , move synapse.app to Applications, and open it. The app is Developer ID signed and notarized, so it opens without a security override and without a right-click workaround. Choose the location before the next step The CLI installed from a packaged app launches the executable inside that signed bundle. Install the CLI only after the app is where you intend to keep it, or the command will point at a path that no longer exists. If you move the app later, the dashboard offers Repair — it recognizes a stale executable path rather than reporting a healthy connection. Install the CLI Open Synapse Settings and choose Install CLI , or run the installer from inside the bundle. Either way it reports where it landed: text Copy Installed /Users/example/.local/bin/synapse Add /Users/example/.local/bin to PATH to use synapse from your shell. Open a new terminal and confirm the shell can find it: shell Copy synapse version synapse path text Copy synapse 1.14.5 text Copy data /Users/example/Library/Application Support/synapse soul /Users/example/Library/Application Support/synapse/SOUL.md cli /Users/example/.local/bin/synapse If the shell cannot find synapse , add ~/.local/bin to PATH and start another shell. The data path above must match what the app reports on its Settings screen — if the two differ, something has set SYNAPSE_DATA in one context and not the other, and they are reading different stores. Connect a detected tool Return to the dashboard. Each supported tool appears as a row with its state. Choose Connect beside Codex, Claude Code, or pi, and the row moves from detected to connected. Connect the others too if you have them — the whole point is one memory behind all of them. Detection is not a guess. Synapse parses the actual entry named synapse in the tool's own configuration and reports connected only when the stored command resolves to the expected executable and its arguments are exactly ["mcp"] . A tool whose binary was deleted or moved reads as stale, not healthy. Know what connecting actually wrote This is worth understanding now rather than the first time something looks wrong. Connecting is not a black box — it is four specific changes, and every one is reversible. Change Where How it is made The MCP server ~/.codex/config.toml or ~/.claude.json Through the tool's own mcp add command, not by editing its file directly. A guidance pointer ~/.codex/AGENTS.md or ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md Appended inside a managed block. Your own text is untouched. A session hook ~/.claude/settings.json Claude Code only. Runs synapse session at session start. A status line ~/.claude/settings.json Claude Code only, and only if you do not already have one. Yours is reported, never replaced. Every changed file gets a .synapsebackup sibling before it is replaced, and the whole operation rolls back if any step fails. Check the shared guidance file was created: shell Copy synapse guidance show text Copy SOUL.md /Users/example/Library/Application Support/synapse/SOUL.md exists true pointers 2/2 consolidated false A full count — pointers 3/3 with all three tools connected — means each one points at a single editable SOUL.md . That file is yours to edit; it is where shared guidance for every connected tool lives. Restart the tool and read its first line Close and reopen the connected tool so it loads the new MCP server. A running session keeps the tool list it started with, so this step is not optional. Claude Code will print a line beside its welcome box before the model has written anything: text Copy Synapse connected · no memories yet That line comes from the session hook, which is the only way to state the connection before the first reply. It also hands the session this project's memory directly, so a Claude Code session starts already holding what the project has decided rather than being asked to go and look. On an empty store there is nothing to hand over yet, which is what you are seeing. Codex has no session hook, so it reports the connection in its first reply instead, following the guidance in SOUL.md . Either way, ask the tool what Synapse tools it has. The answer should include remember , recall , readmemory , and vaultstatus — four core tools. The sixteen mesh tools appear only when you switch the mesh on. Store one memory Tell the connected tool: Remember this confirmed tutorial convention: documentation examples use the source label synapsetutorial. It should call remember with the current project root and report a numeric ID. Use an ordinary convention for this — memory is plain text readable by every connected tool, so never put a token, password, or private key in it. Synapse removes the ones it recognizes before storing and replaces them with [redacted] , but that is a backstop, not a reason to try. Verify the same record three ways One store, three surfaces. Check all of them, because a mismatch here is the clearest signal that something is pointed at the wrong place. shell Copy synapse memory list synapsetutorial text Copy 1 project:/Users/example/project synapsetutorial Documentation examples use the source label synapsetutorial. The columns are the ID, the scope and project it belongs to, the source label, and the body. Now the exact record: shell Copy synapse memory show 1 text Copy Memory #1 Scope: project Project: /Users/example/project Source: synapsetutorial Created: 1785776940 Documentation examples use the source label synapsetutorial. Finally, open the Memories screen in the app and search for synapsetutorial . The body, source, and scope must match what the terminal just printed. At this point the coding tool, the CLI, and the desktop app are provably reading one local database. If something is not right Symptom What it usually means The tool lists no Synapse tools It was not restarted after connecting. Close it fully and reopen. The dashboard row says stale The app moved after the connection was made. Choose Repair . synapse : command not found ~/.local/bin is not on PATH , or the shell has not been restarted. CLI and app show different memory counts They are on different data directories. Compare synapse path with the app's Settings screen. The tool reports a connection that is not there Run synapse doctor . It reports what is actually configured rather than what should be. shell Copy synapse doctor That one command is also what to attach to a bug report. It carries no memory contents and no secret names, so it is safe to paste into a public issue. Undoing all of it shell Copy synapse disconnect claude # or codex, or nothing for every tool Disconnecting removes only what Synapse wrote: the MCP entry, the managed block in the instruction file, the session hook, and the status line — and only if that status line is the one Synapse installed. Your own words in CLAUDE.md , your own status line, and every memory survive it. Removing memory is a separate, explicit decision covered in Check, migrate, and remove Synapse . Next step Continue with Carry one decision between tools to prove a real handoff across a session boundary and a tool boundary.

title: Carry one decision between tools
description: Make a real project convention durable in one session, recover it in another tool after closing the first, correct it at the source, and see the scope rule keep other projects out.
text: Outcome and prerequisites You will prove that durable context survives two boundaries a conversation cannot: the end of a session, and the move to a different tool. Then you will correct it at the source and confirm that another project cannot see it. Install and connect your first tools completed. Two connected tools make the handoff visible. Two separate sessions of one tool prove persistence just as well. A real project folder, and a second one for the scope check. Choose one decision worth keeping Use something concrete, harmless, and genuinely load-bearing for future work. A package-manager choice, a supported deployment target, a naming rule, or a correction to an assumption that turned out wrong are all good. The test of a good memory is whether a session that did not know it would do something different. Worth remembering Not worth remembering "Use Bun for JavaScript tasks in this repository." "The user asked me to check the tests." "Releases are triggered by a version bump on main." "The build is currently failing." "Do not hand-edit the generated site directory." A full transcript of how you reached the decision. The right-hand column is transient. It is true today and misleading next week, and a memory store full of it makes recall worse rather than better. Never stage a fake secret Memory is plain text available to every connected tool. Use an ordinary project convention, never a token, credential, or private key — not even a made-up one, because a habit formed here is a habit that shows up in a real store. Confirm it, then have the tool remember it In the first connected tool, establish the decision explicitly, then ask for it to be stored: We have confirmed that this repository uses Bun for JavaScript tasks. Remember that durable convention with source synapsetutorial. The tool should call remember once, with project scope and this repository's root, and return an ID. Two things can go wrong here and both are worth noticing: It stores a transcript instead of the decision. A memory should be one durable idea in one or two sentences. You will fix this in the correction step. It stores global scope instead of project. Global memory is returned in every project, which is right for a preference about how you like to work and wrong for a fact about one repository. Close the session completely Exit the first tool. Not a new conversation inside it — exit it. This is what rules out conversational context and leaves the local database as the only thing carrying the decision forward. Recall it from the other tool Open the second connected tool in the same repository. If it is Claude Code, look at what happens before you type anything: the session hook has already recalled this project's memory and handed it over, so the convention is in context from the first turn. That is the difference between memory that works and memory that depends on the model remembering to ask. Either way, ask a question the convention should change the answer to: What command should I use to install dependencies here? It should answer with Bun rather than npm, and be able to say where that came from. If it guesses wrong, ask it explicitly to recall the JavaScript tooling convention for this project — that tells you whether the memory is missing or merely was not consulted. Inspect the source of truth and correct it What the tool reported is a rendering. Go and look at the record itself: shell Copy synapse memory list "Bun JavaScript" text Copy 4 project:github.com/example/project synapsetutorial We confirmed together that this repository uses Bun for JavaScript tasks rather than npm, after discussing… shell Copy synapse memory show 4 If the body is a paragraph of conversation rather than a durable statement, replace it. Editing keeps the same ID, so nothing else has to change and no contradicting second record is created: shell Copy printf '%s\n' 'Use Bun for JavaScript tasks in this repository.' \ | synapse memory edit 4 synapsetutorial text Copy Updated memory #4 Start one more new session and ask again. The answer should now reflect the corrected text — which proves that editing changed the durable source rather than layering a correction on top of a wrong record. Correcting beats appending Two memories that disagree are worse than one that is slightly wrong, because recall returns both and the model has to guess which is current. When the wording was bad, edit the record. When the old version was true and stopped being true, add the new one with synapse memory supersede so the old text stays readable but out of recall. Add a plain second memory only when it is genuinely a new fact. Prove other projects cannot see it This is the property that makes a shared store usable. Open a session in an unrelated project and ask the same question: What command should I use to install dependencies here? It must not answer with the first project's convention. Confirm from the terminal that the record is scoped where you think it is: shell Copy synapse memory show 4 text Copy Memory #4 Scope: project Project: github.com/example/project Source: synapsetutorial Recall from any project returns everything global plus everything stored for that project. Another project's memory never enters the response. The project root is resolved by walking up for a .git directory or a .synapse.yaml , so a session opened in a subdirectory still resolves to the same root — which is why the same memory is found whether you start at the repository top or three folders down. The project is then named by the repository's origin remote, which is why it reads github.com/example/project rather than a folder. Clone the repository somewhere else, or open a worktree of it, and a session there recalls the same memory. A folder with no remote is named by its path instead, and memory filed under it stays with that path. Store one thing globally, and see the difference Some things belong everywhere. A preference about how you like to work is not a fact about one repository: shell Copy printf '%s\n' 'Prefer small, focused commits with imperative subject lines.' \ | synapse memory add synapsetutorial --global text Copy Stored memory #5 Now recall from both projects. The global preference appears in each; the Bun convention appears in only one. That split — global plus this project, never another project — is the entire scope model, and it is enforced in the query rather than trusted to the caller. Keep or clean up If the convention is real, keep it — you have just made your tools better at this repository. If it was tutorial-only, remove the exact IDs: shell Copy synapse memory list synapsetutorial synapse memory delete 4 --confirm synapse memory delete 5 --confirm Deleting requires --confirm and names the record it is about to remove. Avoid synapse memory wipe unless you genuinely intend to remove every memory in the store; it exists for starting over, not for tidying. Next step You have finished the newcomer level. Continue with Curate and optimize memory , which is about keeping a store useful once it has more than a handful of entries in it.

title: Curate and optimize memory
description: Build a small memory set, learn how search actually behaves, correct entries at the source, tune the recall budget, import existing notes reversibly, and remove only what you added.
text:
Outcome and prerequisites You will build a small set of entries, understand why search returns what it returns, correct one at the source, compare what each recall budget actually sends to a model, import a Markdown file reversibly, and then undo it. This is the tutorial to read when recall is returning too much, too little, or the wrong thing. The synapse CLI installed and at least one tool connected. A project folder. Steps here create and delete entries under one source label. Write down the IDs Every add prints its new numeric ID. Keep those numbers for the cleanup step. Do not reach for synapse memory wipe in a store that has real context in it — it removes everything, and it is meant for starting over rather than tidying. Add focused entries Content is read from stdin, never from an argument, so a memory can contain anything without shell quoting getting in the way: shell Copy printf '%s
' 'Tutorial apps use port 4100.' | synapse memory add synapsetutorial printf '%s
' 'Tutorial commands use Bun.' | synapse memory add synapsetutorial printf '%s
' 'Tutorial backups go in the backups folder.' | synapse memory add synapsetutorial text Copy Stored memory #1 Stored memory #2 Stored memory #3 synapsetutorial is the source — a label saying where the fact came from. Give every memory one. It is what lets you find a set later, audit what a particular session stored, and delete a batch without hunting. One durable idea per entry. Three entries about ports, runtimes, and backups can each be recalled, corrected, and deleted on their own; one entry containing all three is returned whole every time any part of it is relevant, and cannot be corrected without rewriting the rest. Search and inspect shell Copy synapse memory list tutorial text Copy 2 project:/Users/example/project synapsetutorial Tutorial commands use Bun. 1 project:/Users/example/project synapsetutorial Tutorial apps use port 4100. The columns are the ID, the scope with its project, the source, and the body. For anything scripted, ask for JSON instead: shell Copy synapse memory list "Bun" --json text Copy [ { "id": 2, "body": "Tutorial commands use Bun.", "source": "synapsetutorial", "scope": "project", "project": "/Users/example/project", "created": 1785776940 } ] And for one exact record, with nothing trimmed: shell Copy synapse memory show 2 text Copy Memory #2 Scope: project Project: /Users/example/project Source: synapsetutorial Created: 1785776940 Tutorial commands use Bun. Understand how search behaves Recall is full-text search with a few behaviors worth knowing, because each explains results that otherwise look wrong. Words match in other forms, and so do fragments. The query is searched twice: once by word, stemmed, so deploying finds a memory that says deploys ; and once by three-character pieces, so hashpw finds scripts/hashpw.sh . A memory that matches both ways ranks above one that matches only one. Its source is searched too, at a lower weight, so the label you file a memory under helps find it. shell Copy synapse memory list deploying synapse memory list synapsetutorial Common words are dropped. A query is stripped of words that carry no meaning on their own. Try it: shell Copy synapse memory list "what are the" Nothing in that query survives, so instead of matching every memory containing the , Synapse answers the way it answers an empty query — with the most recent entries. That is deliberate. Matching on a common word is both wrong, because a memory that happens to contain are is not the answer to anything, and slow, because a common word makes the index rank most of the store. An empty query is a real question. It means "what should I know here", and it returns the most recent memory in scope. This is exactly what a session opening asks, and it is what the Claude Code session hook uses. shell Copy synapse memory list Words that carry a preference are kept. not , never , and use look like function words but change the meaning of a convention completely, so they stay in the query. "Never use npm" and "use npm" must not search identically. You can ask what it did. When a memory you know is stored does not come back, the fastest answer is to make the search show its working: shell Copy synapse memory list "what are the credentials" --explain text Copy Query: what are the credentials Mode: search Expression: "credentials" Fragments: "credentials" Searched: credentials Dropped: what, are, the (matches nearly every memory) Matches: 0 That distinguishes the two things that look identical from the outside: a query that lost its only real word, and a store that genuinely holds nothing. And you can skip the ranking entirely. When you want an exact string — a flag, an identifier, a path — the ranked search is the wrong tool, because the thing you are looking for may be a word it drops: shell Copy synapse memory grep -- --no-verify And you can measure it. Once a project has memory worth keeping, write down a few questions you expect it to answer, with text the right answer contains, and score recall against them. Run it again after a cleanup and the numbers say whether the store got easier to search or harder: toml Copy [[case]] query = "which javascript runtime" project = "/Users/example/project" expect = ["bun"] shell Copy synapse memory eval cases.toml Measuring recall explains each number, including how often the answer survived the response budget. Scope is applied in the query, not after it Every search returns everything global plus everything for the current project, and nothing from any other project. That is enforced where the rows are selected rather than filtered afterwards, so there is no path where another project's memory is read and then discarded. Correct at the source A convention becomes more precise. Replace the record rather than adding a second one that disagrees with it: shell Copy printf '%s
' 'Tutorial commands use Bun unless a task requires another runtime.' \ | synapse memory edit 2 synapsetutorial synapse memory show 2 text Copy Updated memory #2 The ID is stable, so anything referring to this memory still refers to the right thing, and future recall returns only the corrected text. Two entries that contradict each other are the single most common way a memory store gets worse as it grows: recall returns both and the model has to guess which is current. Editing is right when the old wording had nothing worth keeping. When the old version was true and then stopped being true , supersede it instead — the new memory becomes the one recall returns, and the old one stays readable as the record of what used to be the case: shell Copy printf '%s
' 'Tutorial commands use Bun. Node is used only for the release script.' \ | synapse memory add synapsetutorial synapse memory supersede 2 6 text Copy Memory #2 superseded by #6; recall now returns #6 instead Undo with: synapse memory restore 2 Check both. Memory 2 is still there, marked, and out of recall; memory 6 is what a tool now sees. If you decide you were wrong, synapse memory restore 2 puts it straight back. shell Copy synapse memory show 2 synapse memory list Tune what recall actually sends The budget controls how much a recall response costs a model in context. Look at where you are: shell Copy synapse settings show text Copy optimization balanced result limit 8 character budget 6000 mesh off shell modes command-scoped, ambient directory zsh hook eval "$(synapse hook zsh)" Budget Results Characters When to use it Full 25 unbounded A small store, or when you want everything and context is cheap. Balanced 8 6,000 The default, and the right answer for most stores. Lean 4 2,800 A large store, a long session, or a model whose context you are protecting. shell Copy synapse settings optimize lean text Copy Recall optimization set to Lean Ask a connected tool to recall synapsetutorial and note how many entries come back. Switch to full and ask again. The stored bodies never change — synapse memory show returns the same text at every setting. The budget only shapes the response. A tool can request a smaller budget for one call, and that request can only ever shrink your configured ceiling. A session cannot talk its way into a larger response than you have allowed. shell Copy synapse settings optimize balanced Import notes you already have If you have been keeping conventions in a Markdown file, bring them in. Every import previews first: shell Copy synapse memory import markdown notes.md text Copy Markdown: 1 found · 1 ready · 0 existing · 0 flagged ready notes.md # Conventions - Use Bun, never npm. - Deploys target Apple silicon only. … Preview only. Add --confirm to import safe entries. Now try one with a credential in it and watch what happens: text Copy Markdown: 1 found · 0 ready · 0 existing · 1 flagged review flagged.md Content hidden until the source file is reviewed. warning: mentions a credential-shaped environment variable Preview only. Add --confirm to import safe entries. Flagged content is not merely skipped — it is not even displayed, because printing it to your terminal to warn you about it would defeat the point. --confirm imports the ready entries and leaves flagged ones untouched. The flagging is conservative, not exhaustive It looks for private-key markers, credential-shaped variable names, assignments to password- and token-like keys, and bearer tokens. A secret that matches none of those patterns will not be caught. Read your own preview — the flag is a safety net, not a substitute for looking. shell Copy synapse memory import markdown notes.md --confirm text Copy Import batch #1: 1 stored, 0 linked, 0 already imported, 0 flagged and left untouched Undo with: synapse memory undo 1 --confirm The entries that are imported are redacted on the way in, like every memory Synapse stores: a credential that slipped past the flag becomes [redacted] rather than being written to the database. Imports are idempotent. Running the same file again reports the entries as already imported rather than creating duplicates, so a repeated import is harmless. Claude and Codex memory stores import the same way with synapse memory import claude and synapse memory import codex . Undo the whole batch shell Copy synapse memory imports text Copy 1 markdown 1 stored 0 linked active shell Copy synapse memory undo 1 --confirm synapse memory imports text Copy Undid import batch #1; removed 1 imported memories text Copy 1 markdown 1 stored 0 linked undone The batch is recorded rather than forgotten, so an import you regret is one command to reverse and the record of it having happened survives. Anything you wrote by hand is untouched — undo removes only what that batch stored. Delete only what you added shell Copy synapse memory list synapsetutorial synapse memory delete 1 --confirm synapse memory delete 2 --confirm synapse memory delete 3 --confirm text Copy Deleted memory #1 Both destructive commands refuse without --confirm , and say which record they mean: text Copy Error: add --confirm to delete memory #3 Error: add --confirm to delete every memory A final synapse memory list synapsetutorial should return nothing. Use the Memories screen for a visual review before deleting anything you did not create in this tutorial. Next step Continue with Use a scoped secret in either shell mode , which is the other half of what Synapse hands a tool — and the half where the boundaries matter most.

title: Use a scoped secret in either shell mode
description: Create a vaulted value, approve its project mapping, compare one-command and ambient loading without ever printing it, and watch trust invalidate the moment the file changes.
text: Outcome and prerequisites You will create a disposable value in the vault, map it to one project, and exercise both ways Synapse can hand it to something — without the value ever appearing on screen. Then you will break the approval on purpose and watch every path refuse. The synapse CLI installed. If synapse vault backend says keychain , unlock your login Keychain first. An empty temporary folder. Do not run this in a real project. About twenty-five minutes. Where the value actually lives Worth being precise about before you start, because the whole design follows from it. Thing Stored where The secret value The value store, and only there. That is vault.db — sealed, one envelope per secret, under the key in vault.key — or macOS Keychain if the machine is set to it. synapse vault backend says which. Its name, its variable name, its account reference brain.db , Synapse's SQLite database. Never the value. Which variable a folder should get .synapse.yaml in the project, which holds a reference and never a value. Whether that file is trusted A SHA-256 digest of its exact bytes, recorded when you approve it. No secret value is ever written to brain.db , to YAML, to an MCP response, or to a log, and neither store keeps one in plaintext. A value is read out of the vault at the moment a child process is launched, and goes nowhere else unless you ask for it with synapse secret copy , which puts it on the clipboard and still never prints it. Create a vault and a value shell Copy mkdir -p "$HOME/tmp/synapsetutorial" cd "$HOME/tmp/synapsetutorial" synapse vault create tutorial synapse secret set tutorial demo SYNAPSE_TUTORIAL_TOKEN Enter a disposable value at the hidden prompt and confirm it. A vault is an organizational label; the three arguments are the vault, the secret's name inside it, and the environment variable it will become. text Copy Created vault tutorial Saved tutorial.demo in the encrypted vault Now list what exists. Metadata only — there is no command that prints a value, because there is no reason for one to exist: shell Copy synapse secret list tutorial text Copy tutorial.demo SYNAPSE_TUTORIAL_TOKEN scoped Secrets are never command arguments synapse secret set reads from a TTY prompt or stdin, never from an argument. An argument would land in your shell history, in the process table, and in any terminal recording — three places a value should never be. Map it to this folder and approve the file shell Copy synapse scope init . Replace the generated .synapse.yaml with: yaml Copy version: 1 scope: project env: SYNAPSE_TUTORIAL_TOKEN: tutorial.demo deny: [] tutorial.demo is a reference, not a value. This file is safe to commit — that is the point of it holding a reference. Look at the file, then approve its exact bytes: shell Copy synapse scope status . synapse allow synapse status . text Copy Allowed /Users/example/tmp/synapsetutorial/.synapse.yaml text Copy Folder: . Available: SYNAPSE_TUTORIAL_TOKEN Ambient: ready /Users/example/tmp/synapsetutorial/.synapse.yaml [project · approved] Ambient: ready means a shell hook would activate here. It does not mean one is installed. Hand it to exactly one command This is the narrower of the two boundaries and the one to prefer. Verify presence without printing content: shell Copy synapse run -- sh -c 'test -n "$SYNAPSE_TUTORIAL_TOKEN" && echo "tutorial token available"' The child prints only the fixed sentence. Confirm the parent shell was never touched: shell Copy test -z "$SYNAPSE_TUTORIAL_TOKEN" && echo "parent unchanged" Synapse read the stored value, set it on that one child, and the child exited with it. Nothing was exported into your session. The child is fully trusted with the value Any process launched through synapse run can read and disclose what it is given. This tutorial uses a disposable value and a child that only tests whether it is non-empty. The boundary Synapse enforces is which processes receive a value, not what they do with it afterwards. Activate the whole directory For a permanent setup, use Settings → Shell environments → Enable shell hook and open a new terminal. To try it immediately in this shell: shell Copy # zsh eval "$(synapse hook zsh)" # bash: eval "$(synapse hook bash)" # fish: synapse hook fish | source The approved scope activates at once. Now walk in and out of it: shell Copy test -n "$SYNAPSE_TUTORIAL_TOKEN" && echo "ambient token available" cd .. test -z "$SYNAPSE_TUTORIAL_TOKEN" && echo "ambient token unloaded" cd synapsetutorial test -n "$SYNAPSE_TUTORIAL_TOKEN" && echo "ambient token restored" All three print. Leaving the directory unloads exactly the variables the hook loaded — and if one of them had a value before activation, leaving restores that original value rather than unsetting it. The hook tracks which keys it owns precisely so it can put things back as it found them. The entire shell is trusted now Every process launched from this shell can read the value, including ones you did not think about. Prefer synapse run for anything sensitive, and keep shell tracing off while the hook evaluates — a traced shell prints what it is setting. Break the approval and watch everything refuse Approval is bound to the exact bytes of the file. A blank line is a different file: shell Copy echo "" >> .synapse.yaml synapse status . text Copy Folder: . Available: none Ambient: blocked /Users/example/tmp/synapsetutorial/.synapse.yaml [project · pending] warning: /Users/example/tmp/synapsetutorial/.synapse.yaml: Scope has not been approved Three things happen at once. Ambient mode unloads at the next prompt. synapse run refuses before launching anything. And synapse launch refuses to start a coding tool at all: shell Copy synapse run -- sh -c 'echo should-not-run' text Copy Error: vault scope is not ready: /Users/example/tmp/synapsetutorial/.synapse.yaml: Scope has not been approved It refuses rather than running with the variable missing, because a command that runs against a half-resolved environment fails in ways that look like success. Read what changed, then re-approve: shell Copy synapse scope status . synapse allow Both presence tests work again. This is what makes a committed .synapse.yaml safe: a teammate's edit, or a malicious one, arrives untrusted and stays that way until a human looks at it. Prove that deny wins Scopes resolve from the root of your filesystem down to the current folder, so a narrower file can add variables. It can never add back one a broader scope denied. Move the variable into deny : yaml Copy version: 1 scope: project env: {} deny: - SYNAPSE_TUTORIAL_TOKEN shell Copy synapse allow synapse status . Available no longer lists the name. Create a folder-level scope beneath this one that tries to map it again, approve that too, and it still will not appear. Deny is a ceiling, not a default. See why global is not the same as ambient A secret can be marked global, meaning it is available without any scope file naming it: shell Copy synapse secret global tutorial.demo on synapse secret list tutorial text Copy tutorial.demo is now global text Copy tutorial.demo SYNAPSE_TUTORIAL_TOKEN global Now move to a folder with no .synapse.yaml at all and check: shell Copy cd ~ && synapse status . text Copy Folder: . Available: SYNAPSE_TUTORIAL_TOKEN Ambient: inactive Read those two lines together, because the difference between them is a deliberate safety property. The name is available — synapse run here would provide it. But ambient is inactive : a shell hook will not load it, because an ambient environment never activates from a global mapping alone. Turning on a global secret cannot silently populate every shell you open. shell Copy synapse secret global tutorial.demo off Check what a connected tool can actually see Go back to the tutorial folder and ask a connected coding tool to call vaultstatus . It reports the variable names available here, the trust state of each scope, and whether ambient mode is ready — and no values, because that tool has no code path that reads one. The same is true of a preview. synapse launch claude --print shows DEMO_TOKEN=<from the vault> rather than a redacted value, because a preview calls a different function that lists names and never opens the vault at all. There is no value in the process to leak. Clean up shell Copy synapse deny synapse secret forget tutorial.demo synapse vault delete tutorial cd .. && rm -rf synapsetutorial text Copy Forgot tutorial.demo Deleted vault tutorial The next prompt unloads the ambient value. Forgetting the secret removes the stored value and Synapse's record of it, from both stores rather than only the one in use — so a machine that has switched backends leaves nothing behind in the one it stopped reading. What you can rely on Secret values never reach brain.db , YAML, an MCP response, or a log, and are never at rest in plaintext.
